> Dear INLA experts,
>

>

>
>

>

Hi Finn,

Would this also work for a survival model where we have both a dependant variable "y" and a censoring variable "cens"? I would imagine that i follow the procedure and create the observation matrices for both the "y" and "cens"? Or is it sufficient to only do this for y and let "cens" be a 1 x (n+m) matrix where n is the normal data and m is the boundary observations?

Best regards,
Michael

Den mån 31 okt. 2022 kl 22:18 skrev Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com>:

> With control.inla you would need a separate likelihood for the special
> "observations".
> But there's also a "scale" parameter to inla() itself, that _might_ be
> useful, in that you can set a large scaling factor for the precision
> for those particular "observations".
> However, since they will still be involved in the parameter
> estimation, I would worry that they would influence the precision
> estimates too much, so the multi-likelihood options seems much safer.
>
> You just need to make the observation variable a matrix.
> Instead of y = c(ordinary_obs, special_obs), use
> y=rbind(cbind(ordinary_obs, NA), cbind(NA, special_obs)) .
> (that's for plain inla; in inlabru, that matrix is constructed
> automatically when building multi-likelihood models, so you don't need
> the NA stuff there).
>
> Then
>   family = c("gaussian", "gaussian")
> and
>   control.family = list(list(...), list(...))
> containing the two separate hyper-definitions.
>
> Finn
>
> On Mon, 31 Oct 2022 at 15:22, michael <sederli...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi!
> >

> >
> > Is this something that can be done easily?
> >
> > Best regards,

messages.subject: Assessing Predictive Performance
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have seen several posts about using cpo/pit for model selection, but what is the appropriate metric to use when assessing the accuracy of predictions from a selected model? and how is that metric graded?

i.e. I am not comparing models but trying to quantify how well my final model is doing at making predictions.

Many thanks,
Sylvan

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Assessing Predictive Performance
messages.body_plain:
This depends on the type of prediction.

There are general scores one can use, _given_ a specific quantity to
be predicted.
leave-one-out cross validation is just one type of prediction
quantity, and it may not be the most appropriate for real situations.

But once you've figured out what quantity you care about prediction
for, then you can choose between a range of metrics. Normally, proper
scoring rules are preferable, as they guarantee that the (expected)
score won't be better than the (expected) score for the "true"
prediction distribution.  Whether there exists such as a thing as the
"true" prediction distribution doesn't really matter; the proper score
property says that for a forecast F and prediction score S(F,y) for
observed y, the expectation S(F,G) = E_{y~G}[S(F,y)] fulfills S(F,G)
\geq S(G,G) for _any_ distribution G (so it could be the full data
generating distribution or some "optimal" prediction distribution;
it's unknown, but the expectectation relation holds for all G).  So if
you use some proper score for assessment, you can't "cheat" by
altering the predictions to e.g. artificially lower the prediction
variance; your score will not be better (on average).  For strictly
proper scores, _any_ difference between F and G shows up in the
expectations, but more common merely proper scores are only sensitive
to some properties; e.g. squared error only cares about the posterior
mean, and absolute median error only cares about the posterior median.
The -log-likelihood score is strictly proper.

I've started a vignette about prediction scores, and how to use
posterior sampling to access the needed posterior distribution
quantities in some situations, here:
https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/prediction_scores.html
(the predict() calls simply call inla.posterior.sample() internally,
and summarise the results, so the same principles can be used with
plain INLA estimates)

It doesn't cover how to choose what quantities to assess prediction
_for_, but hopefully still gives some answers to your question.

Finn

messages.subject: Mixture Models and Coregionalization
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am currently fitting bivariate coregionalization models using INLA. However, the fit is not good in the tail, so I am thinking of combining the coregionalization model with a mixture model (for bulk and tail) and fit them both using INLA.
I understand that mixture models don't have a GMRF representation and must be conditioned to be fitted in INLA following the INLA within MCMC framework. Is it possible to fit an INLA coregionalization model within MCMC? My thinking is to use MCMC to produce the fixed parameters and use the INLA coregionalization model on the data conditioned on the fixed parameters. Am I correct? Do you think it is possible? I am looking for reasons why it wouldn't be, and can't see any.

Thank you for your help, oh INLA oracle.

Daniela

messages.subject_clean: Simulation Question about INLA Binomial Model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I ran a INLA-SPDE model using the binomial family, and was trying to carry out a simulation study using results from inla.posterior.sample to simulate the numbers of zeros and ones to compare to the observed numbers of zeros and ones in my dataset.

When using the following code, below, I found the results to be opposite to what I expected. My dataset has approximately 20,000 zeros and 5,000 ones, but my simulations were producing close to 20,000 ones and 5,000 zeros.

Is there something wrong with my simulation code for "mu", or how I set the probability using "rbinom"? Or is the model performing that poorly?

If anyone could provide any help, it would be much appreciated.

Sincerely,

Kristin

Nsim=1000

Sim <- inla.posterior.sample(n = Nsim, result = Top_model_config)
numrows <- nrow(Sim[[1]]$latent)

BetaNum <- rownum1
#Determines rows for each fixed effect
SpatialNum <- rownum3
#Determines rows for each mesh node
Day <- rownum7
#Determines rows for each day

N <- nrow(data.df)
X <- data.frame(Intercept = rep(1, N),
                VarA = data.df$VarA,
               VarB = data.df$VarB,
                VarC = data.df$VarC,
                VarD = data.df$VarD,
                VarE = data.df$VarE)

Xm <- as.matrix(X)

spatial_sim <- matrix(nrow=N, ncol=Nsim) #Create a matrix to hold our 1000 model realizations, one in each column
Zeros <- vector(length = Nsim)
#Create 1000 sets of simulated responses from the model realizations
mu.i <- matrix(nrow = N, ncol = Nsim)
Am   <- as.matrix(A_point)
for (i in 1: Nsim){
  Betas     <- Sim[[i]]$latent[as.numeric(BetaNum)]
  spatials  <- Sim[[i]]$latent[as.numeric(SpatialNum)]
  Day <- Sim[[i]]$latent[Day]
  FixedPart <- Xm %*% Betas + Am %*% spatials + Day[data.df$DAY]
 mu.i[,i]  <- exp(FixedPart)/( 1 + exp(FixedPart))
  spatial_sim[,i] <- rbinom(n = N, size = 1, prob = mu.i)
  Zeros[i] <- sum(spatial_sim[,i] ==0)
}

messages.body_plain:
Let me describe my problem in detail.
Suppose A is a large island with 30 administrative areas. b is a small island with only three administrative areas. c is an even smaller island with only one administrative area. In the paper "A note on intrinsic conditional autoregressive models for disconnected graphs", it is described in detail how to handle this situation. But now I want to generate simulated data of spatially structured random effects for these islands. As you said, it is possible to sample A,B,C separately. But I think that even though A,B are not geographically connected, there should be some correlation between the spatial random effects of the two islands if they are in close proximity. The basis is as follows: Suppose that island A has three regions a, b, and c. A is adjacent to b, b is adjacent to c, and a is connected to c through b but not adjacent to it. Although a and c are not adjacent to each other, the spatial effects of the two can be transmitted through b, i.e., there is still some correlation. Therefore the region on island A and the region on island B should still have some correlation even though they are not adjacent to each other.

messages.body_plain:
A common approach is to just add some extra graph edge to connect the islands.
Another approach is to add a separate model component that just has a single value for each island, that models only the island averages; this would be a standard multi-level modelling approach.

Finn

> On 3 Nov 2022, at 08:09, newer <wenlo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ﻿Let me describe my problem in detail.

>
> Suppose A is a large island with 30 administrative areas. b is a small island with only three administrative areas. c is an even smaller island with only one administrative area. In the paper "A note on intrinsic conditional autoregressive models for disconnected graphs", it is described in detail how to handle this situation. But now I want to generate simulated data of spatially structured random effects for these islands. As you said, it is possible to sample A,B,C separately. But I think that even though A,B are not geographically connected, there should be some correlation between the spatial random effects of the two islands if they are in close proximity. The basis is as follows: Suppose that island A has three regions a, b, and c. A is adjacent to b, b is adjacent to c, and a is connected to c through b but not adjacent to it. Although a and c are not adjacent to each other, the spatial effects of the two can be transmitted through b, i.e., there is still some correlation. Therefore the region on island A and the region on island B should still have some correlation even though they are not adjacent to each other.
>

messages.body_plain:
I have been trying to convert my inla call to a bru call to use some of the inlabru wrappers like generate() and predict(), but am having some issues. My model looks like this:

```
model <- inla(target ~ 1

    + fixed_effect_1
    + fixed_effect_2
    + fixed_effect_3
    + fixed_effect_4
    + fixed_effect_5
    + fixed_effect_6
    + fixed_effect_7

    # Random Effects
    + f(random_effect_1, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_1)
    + f(random_effect_2, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_2)
    + f(random_effect_3, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_3)
    + f(random_effect_4, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_4)
    + f(random_effect_5, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_5)
    + f(random_effect_6, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_6)
    + f(random_effect_7, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_7)
    + f(random_effect_8, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_8)

    , data=modeling_df, family="T"
    , control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, po=TRUE, config=TRUE)
    , control.inla=list(strategy="adaptive",  int.strategy="auto", cmin=0)
    , verbose=F
)
```

I have tried various ways, but do not think I am close to getting it to work. How can I convert this to a bru() call?

Thank you.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
that model should only need very minor changes:
(For speed of writing I call the effects rf#, but you could also call them
  random_effect_#, so that other post-processing code you have
wouldn't need to change;
  I assume your actual model has different names for all of the components...)

```
model <- bru(~ Intercept(1)

    + fixed_effect_1
    + fixed_effect_2
    + fixed_effect_3
    + fixed_effect_4
    + fixed_effect_5
    + fixed_effect_6
    + fixed_effect_7

    # Random Effects

    + rf1(random_effect_1, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_1)
    + rf2(random_effect_2, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_2)
    + rf3(random_effect_3, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_3)
    + rf4(random_effect_4, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_4)
    + rf5(random_effect_5, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_5)
    + rf6(random_effect_6, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_6)
    + rf7(random_effect_7, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_7)
    + rf8(random_effect_8, model='iid', hyper=hyper_random_effect_8),
  like(
     formula = target ~ .,
     data=modeling_df, family="T"
  ),
  options = list(
    control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, po=TRUE),

    control.inla=list(strategy="adaptive",  int.strategy="auto", cmin=0),

    verbose=FALSE
  )
)
```

messages.body_plain:
Yes, bru is more picky about the inputs and the default component mappings don’t accept missing covariates. In plain inla, those are treated as “zero effect”, which can
either be achieved by a custom mapper that allows that (I’ll add that to the default mapper to iid models ), or by replacing the NA by e.g. 1, and adding a
weights=!is.na <http://is.na>(original_covariate)
argument to the component definition.
The latter method is available right now.
Once I’ve updated the default iid mapper that will be available in the development version.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
No, it should all be part of each individual component definition;

~ ... + your_component_label(input_without_na, weights =
!is.na <http://is.na>(original_input_with_na), model = "iid", ...)

It also depends a bit on _why_ you have NAs in your random effect
indices.  The method above only applies to the specific case where you
want an NA to lead to "effect = zero".

The reason inlabru doesn't (yet) have that behaviour is that it risks
masking problems where there wasn't supposed to be any missing
covariate values, and then giving effect zero without warning leads to
hard to track down errors in the statistical analysis.  For purely
indexed component types like iid however, it's a different situation
than for may other types of covariates, so the risk of allowing this
behaviour should be smaller, and there are valid use cases.  In the
future however, there will be more complex inlabru component types
where the above explicit !is.na <http://is.na>() solution will be a much clearer
solution than special treatment of NAs, so we'll see how this evolves.
It would help to get some information about your specific use case, so
we can take valid use cases into account when developing the interface
further.

In the CRAN inlabru version (2.6.0) you can probably already simplify
your code by just doing this:

~ ... + comp_label(input_with_na, model="iid", mapper =
bru_mapper_index(n = max(input_with_na, na.rm = TRUE)), ...)

In the development version, I've just modified the default mapper to
allow NA inputs to generate effect zero, so if you install from github
(or in about an hour or so, from
https://inlabru-org.r-universe.dev/ui#package:inlabru when it builds
version 2.6.0.9003) you shouldn't need to do anything special to get
the NA --> zero effects.

Finn

~ ... + comp_label(input_with_na, model="iid", mapper =

I think you mean 0.2*0.31 and not 0.2/0.31, as I changed below. I also
put 'y' into the data.frame

library(INLA)
library(sp)
library(spdep)
####read map

### generate matrix

nb2INLA(paste("rus.map.nb.adj"), rus.map.nb)
rus.adj <- inla.read.graph("rus.map.nb.adj")
###read data

inc$y <- inc$num_positi
inc$region <- 1:nrow(inc)

#########

                       graph = rus.adj,
                       scale.model = T,
                       constr = TRUE,
                       hyper = list(
                         phi = list(
                      prior = 'pc',
                      param = c(0.5,2/3) ,
                      initial = -3),
                        prec = list(
                          prior = 'pc.prec',

### >>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>vvvvvvvv
                          param = c(0.2*0.31, 0.01),

                        initial = 5)))
##########
result <- inla(f_car, family = "poisson", data = inc, E=E,
               control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
               verbose = T)
summary(result)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] spatial modeling with islands
messages.body_plain:
It looks like point A and B are connected; the resolution of your map indicates A and B are on the same island. But C is clearly on a different island, which makes the barrier model isolate it from A and B. In your case, the ocean is acting as the barrier.
If A and B are not one the same island and you want them to be disconnected, you would need to increase the map and mesh resolution so that it can see that A and B are really on different islands.

Finn

> On 5 Nov 2022, at 09:27, newer <wenlo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ﻿Thank you for your reply. I also thought at first that this could be solved by a barrier model. Barrier models are usually used in marine species distribution studies, where islands act as barriers and different r （fields parameter） are set for the ocean and islands, respectively, and two points on either side of the island are connected through the perimeter of the island (i.e., the shortest path). However, the following highlighted words in this literature 《Accounting for Physical Barriers in Species Distribution Modeling With NonStationary Spatial Random Effects》 are not very understandable to me, And it makes me think that barrier models are not suitable for my kind of situation. Because there can't be any physical connection between the two islands.And I have run the code for the barrier model, and the result below is a prior spatial distribution of the correlation, and on the right is the prior for the barrier model. One doubt is that empirically the distance between point A and point B and the distance between point A and point C are basically the same, and also have similar width of the ocean, and the correlation between points B-A and points C-A should be similar, but why the actual result is so different.

messages.subject: spatial modeling with islands
messages.body_plain:
Hi, inla team

     When I model the spatial distribution of diseases, I need to consider spatially structured random effects, and usually introduce matern fields as random effects. However, the field is stationary and isotropic. What I would like to ask is whether there is a way to take this into account when the study area is an archipelago, where the correlation between a point on one island A and another island B is weakened by the presence of the ocean?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Problem with the use of inla.make.lincombs in Linear mixed model
messages.subject_clean: Problem with the use of inla.make.lincombs in Linear mixed model
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA Developers,
I am simply coding a linear mixed model with INLA (see the code below).

LMM_lin_inla <- inla(y ~ age + f(ID, model = "iid"),
                     data = data1, family = "gaussian",
                     control.compute = list(mlik=TRUE, dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, return.marginals.predictor=TRUE),
                     control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE))
summary(LMM_lin_inla)

I would love to have the distibutions of the marginal predictions (so the predictions of the general mean without the random effects). So I tried to use the inla.make.lincombs function but when I run the code it doesn't come to an end. It doesn't give me an output or either an error, after a while R simply stops working.

The code is this:
lc <- inla.make.lincombs("(Intercept)" = rep(1, nrow(data1)), age = data1$age)
# or lc <- model.matrix(~ age, data = data1) %>% as.data.frame() %>% inla.make.lincombs()

LMM_lin_inla <- inla(y ~ age + f(ID, model = "iid"),
                     data = data1, family = "gaussian",
                    control.compute = list(mlik=TRUE, dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, return.marginals.predictor=TRUE),
                  control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE),
                     lincomb = lc,
                    control.inla = list(lincomb.derived.correlation.matrix = TRUE),  verbose = TRUE)

Do you have any suggestions on how to overcome this problem? What do you think is the issue?

Thank in advance for your patient. I hope I gave all the necessary information.
Chiara

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

That would be great!

I have been testing this but been unable to get the observation approach to work in a survival model. It seems to interpret the censoring indicators as well as the observation matrix as observations and complain that the "the number of families 2 does not match number of response variables 6" where my y-variable has dim 2x(N+M) and cens  has size 1 x (N + M).

But.
If I may ask a question about the masking implementation of the Dirichlet condition.
In the example code provided earlier (appended below)  we make a call to inla.spde2.generic directly. It would be very useful to be able to fix the range and standard deviation to better understand the model behaviour.
In the newer implementation inla.spde.pcmatern this would be done by providing prior.range = c(prior.val, NA) and prior.sigma = c(prior.val, NA).

I have not managed to figure out how to achieve this in the implementation below, but would it be straight-forward?

Best regards,
Michael

```
library(INLA)

dirichlet.mask <- function(mesh)
{
  mask <- rep(TRUE, mesh$n)
  mask[unique(mesh$segm$bnd$idx)] <- FALSE
  mask
}

dirichlet.fem <- function(mesh, order=2)
{
  output <- c("c0", "c1",
              paste("k", seq_len(order), sep = ""))
  fem <- inla.fmesher.smorg(mesh$loc, mesh$graph$tv, fem = order,
                            output = output)
  mask <- dirichlet.mask(mesh)
  fem$c0 <- fem$c0[mask,mask,drop=FALSE]
  fem$c1 <- fem$c1[mask,mask,drop=FALSE]
  for (idx in seq_len(order)) {
    fem[[paste("g", idx, sep = "")]] <-
      fem[[paste("k", idx, sep = "")]][mask,mask,drop=FALSE]
  }
  fem
}

matern.dirichlet <- function(mesh, B.tau, B.kappa,
                             theta.mu <http://theta.mu>=rep(0, ncol(B.tau)-1),
                             theta.Q=diag(ncol(B.tau)-1))
{
  fem <- dirichlet.fem(mesh)
  inla.spde2.generic(M0=fem$c0, M1=fem$g1, M2=fem$g2,
                     B0=B.tau, B1=2*B.kappa,
                     B2=cbind(1, B.tau[,-1,drop=FALSE]*0.0),
                     theta.mu <http://theta.mu>=theta.mu <http://theta.mu>, theta.Q=theta.Q,
                     transform="identity")
}

dirichlet.A <- function(mesh, ...)
{
  A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, ...)
  A[, dirichlet.mask(mesh), drop=FALSE]
}

########################################################################

prior.sd <http://prior.sd> <- 1 ## Change this to something reasonable for your problem
prior.range <- 5 ## Change this to something reasonable for your problem

## For parameterisation details, see Eq (4) and onwards in
## Lindgren & Rue, "Bayesian Spatial Modelling with R-INLA,
## Journal of Statistical Software, 2015
## (also as the "read this first" spde tutorial on r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org>)
log.kappa0 <- log(8)/2 - log(prior.range)
log.tau0 <- -log(4*pi)/2 - log(prior.sd <http://prior.sd>) - log.kappa0
B.tau <- cbind(log.tau0, -1, 1)
B.kappa <- cbind(log.kappa0, 0, -1)
theta.mu <http://theta.mu> <- c(0, 0)
theta.prec <- c(0.1, 1)
theta.Q <- diag(theta.prec, length(theta.mu <http://theta.mu>))

lattice <- inla.mesh.lattice(1:30, 1:20)
mesh <- inla.mesh.create(lattice=lattice, extend=FALSE)

## Create a Neumann model
spdeN <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh, B.tau=B.tau, B.kappa=B.kappa,
                           theta.prior.mean=theta.mu <http://theta.mu>,
                           theta.prior.prec=theta.prec)
## Create a Dirichlet model
spdeD <- matern.dirichlet(mesh, B.tau=B.tau, B.kappa=B.kappa,
                          theta.mu <http://theta.mu>=theta.mu <http://theta.mu>,
                          theta.Q=theta.Q)
```

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Future prediction
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
You need to make sure your model goes to 100 days, and not just to 91
days, i.e. ngroup = 100.

Are you using plain INLA or inlabru? inlabru has a predict() function
that internally uses posterior sampling.
But you can also extract the posterior distribution summaries for
individual model components from $summary.random$... if you've set up
the model size correctly.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Boundary constraints in spatial models
messages.body_plain:
Yes, to fix tau and kappa you just need to let B.tau and B.kappa only
have a single column, which gives the log(tau) and log(kappa) values.
For other parameterisations (sigma and range), you just need to work
out the transformation.
When you already have B.tau and B.kappa for a given parameterisation,
and you want to fix the theta vector to some theta0, then you need
B.tau.fixed <- B.tau[, 1, drop = FALSE] + B.tau[, -1, drop = FALSE] %*% theta0
B.kappa.fixed <- B.kappa[, 1, drop = FALSE] + B.kappa[, -1, drop =
FALSE] %*% theta0

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

I see! It is not trivial (to me at least: ) ) to get a thorough understanding of the inner workings on R-INLA.

So my understanding so far is that we implement the boundary condition through masking the mesh nodes in the fem - objects created by fmesher.smorg. Normally this is called in inla.spde2.matern which then calls inla.spde2.generic.
I would like to use the pc-matern prior with the parametrisation prior.range = c(rho0, prho) and prior.sigma = c(sigma0, psigma)  and have the ability to fix these parameters for debugging and understanding the model (as I mentioned before).

So, as far as I now understand it would be possible to create modified versions of inla.spde2.pcmatern and inla.spde2.matern which perform the masking and output the model object to achieve this?

I have appended code of a small example with the modified functions inla.dirichlet.spde2.pcmatern and inla.dirichlet.spde2.matern in dirichlet.R and a simple test case in dirichlet_model_test.R
The only change is that the masking vector is provided as an input to pcmatern which is further passed to matern() which performs the masking before creating the spde model object with the default inla.spde2.generic()

>From the testing I have done, this seems to work ok. But it would also be very comforting with a confirmation that I have not misunderstood.

It uses INLA 22.05.03
"This is INLA_22.05.03 built 2022-05-03 07:58:22 UTC.
 - See www.r-inla.org/contact-us <http://www.r-inla.org/contact-us> for how to get help."

All the best,
Michael

messages.subject: INLA for Skewed Distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have some data where the dependent variable is best described by a skewed Student-T distribution. (It is not centered on zero, has right skew, etc...)

INLA has the Student-T family.  But, I don't see anything that would handle the skew.  Do I need to "T standardize" my dependent variable first? Or, is there another way to handle this?

I was wondering what you think of the following options:
Just fit the model with the T family and skewed dependent variable
Un-skew the dependent variable, using a form of Box-Cox for T distribution
Normalize the dependent variable to Guassian and fit a standard normal mode

Additionally, given the three choices above, what would be the best model summary statistic to determine the "best" one?

Any ideas or suggestions would be greatly appreciate.

Thank You!!!

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA for Skewed Distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hi Noah,

since the observation family applies to the _conditional_ distribution
of the response/dependent variable (or to the regression residuals in
the case of additive error observation families) and not to the
marginal distribution, neither of those options would directly help
with your problem.
In some cases, transforming the marginal distribution of the data as
in your option 2 may be sensible, but that's highly problem dependent.

I would suggest trying option 1 and then looking at the residuals to
see how skewed they are; this is not something one can tell from the
raw observation data; it is a model output.
If the residuals aren't very skewed, it's likely ok. If they are, you
would need to consider further options. (I have some in mind, but they
would be research projects, so not available off-the-shelf...)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
deviance residuals, in the frequentist sense, are defined as

	sign * sqrt(saturated.deviance)

where 'sign' is usually taken as the sign of y-y.predicted

all this is pr observation, so I avoid the _i notation.

In the Bayesian framework, there is no natural definition of residuals,
but we can define it as

	sign * sqrt(E(saturated.deviance))

where the E() is over the posterior, like integrating out
hyperparameter(s) and the uncertainty of the linear predictor.

the 'sign' is a different story, as there is no definition of the 'sign'
now. it is defined as attached, which is 'very likely' in correspondance
with the freq.definition. Another issue, is that I do not know, in this
part of the code, if data are discrete or not, so...

well, I know all this is a little 'loose', but it is anyhow useful to
have some kind of 'residuals' available, although they should not be
used for any kind of ''testing''-purpose.

of'course, for some models, like binary data, then all this make less
sense, but this is well know

If anyone has other options or other comments, please let us know

Best
H

messages.subject: Did I fit my gamma and log-link function model correctly ?
messages.subject_clean: Did I fit my gamma and log-link function model correctly ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA-users,

First I would like to thanks the people that create and interact on this forum! Soo helpful!!

I am trying to model fish biomass according to the distance to marine protected area center. I used an SPDE with a mesh and I assumed a gamma distribution of this relationship (since positive integers, and log link function). I finally managed to have results. However as I am not an expert, I preferred to check with you guys that I did everything correctly.

I first created a mesh based on inla.mesh.2d function
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(Loc,
                      max.edge = c(1, 5) * MaxEdge,
                      cutoff = MaxEdge / 5)

Set the model as following (based on https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-spatial.html#sec:irrlattice):

# 1. inla.spde2.matern: create an object for a Matérn model
vermeille.spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha = 2)

# 2. inla.spde.make.A: create the projector matrix "A" to map the projection of the SPDE to the observed points
A.vermeille <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coordinates(dat))

# 3. inla.spde.make.index: create a necessary list of named index vectors for the SPDE model
s.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name = "spatial.field",
  n.spde = vermeille.spde$n.spde)

4. Stack those items:
vermeille.stack <- inla.stack(data  = list(Mbiomass = dat$Mbiomass),
  A = list(A.vermeille, 1),
  effects = list(c(s.index, list(Intercept = 1)),
    list(Distance = dat$Distance)),
  tag = "vermeille.data")

5. create a prediction based on the grid:
A.pred <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coordinates(vermeille.grid))

vermeille.stack.pred <- inla.stack(data = list(Mbiomass = NA),
                                   A = list(A.pred, 1),
                                   effects = list(c(s.index, list (Intercept = 1)),
                                                  list(Distance = vermeille.grid$Distance)),
                                   tag = "vermeille.pred")

#Join stack
join.stack <- inla.stack(vermeille.stack, vermeille.stack.pred)

6. define my model:
form <- Mbiomass ~ -1 + Intercept + Distance + f(spatial.field, model = spde)

7. fit my model:
m2 <- inla(form, data = inla.stack.data(join.stack, spde = vermeille.spde),
  family = "gamma",
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(join.stack), compute = TRUE,link=1),
  control.compute = list(cpo = TRUE, dic = TRUE),
  control.family=list(link="log"))

 First question: Is it the right way to write the INLA model with gamma family and log-linked function? inla function is the only place I need to inform the model of this distribution?
I am not sure since I also saw https://github.com/tulliapadellini/INLA-quantreg that wrote:

 control.family = list(control.link = list(model = "..."))

What is the difference between

control.family=list(link="log"))
and
control.family = list(control.link = list(model = "..."))

Second question:
At the beginning I did not put link=1 since I thought there is one family. But it says:

m2 <- inla(form, data = inla.stack.data(join.stack, spde = vermeille.spde),
  family = "gamma",
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(join.stack), compute = TRUE),
  control.compute = list(cpo = TRUE, dic = TRUE),
  control.family=list(link="log"))
"*** Warning *** You might want to consider to setting ``control.predictor=list(link=...)''
*** Warning *** otherwise the identity link will be used to compute the fitted values for NA data"

Why should I precise this  link = 1 ?

Thanks a lot in advance for your help.

Charlotte

messages.subject: How to take the difference of marginals.fitted.values from two
messages.subject_clean: How to take the difference of marginals.fitted.values from two
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am trying to produce the posterior difference of marginals.fitted.values from two SPDE models.

Both models have been fitted to the same spatial points but have used data from two different years. I am interested in knowing whether the prevalence of a disease changed between the two time points. Hence I have opted to do the difference of the posteriors of the  marginals.fitted.values from the two models.

I thought this would be a simple subtraction but the structure of the marginals.fitted.values does not allow this.

Any guidance will be appreciated and sorry I may have used wrong terminology I am new in the field.

My naive approach that did not work, below:
model1$marginals.fitted.values[index] - model2$marginals.fitted.values[index]

Regards,
McEwen Khundi.

messages.subject: Preferential sampling with both random and fixed effects
messages.subject_clean: Preferential sampling with both random and fixed effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to implement a model of preferential sampling.  The information I can find on-line is very helpful but I think falls a little short of where I would like to be.  I'm happy with the marked-point-process (two likelihoods) and I'm happy with using f(.,copy='i', .), but I'd also like to "copy" the fixed effects and have them share a common preference parameter.

This could be a little vague, let me try to firm things up a bit.

Let Y be the marks at sites X.  Model the intensity of the LGCP for X as:

log( E(X|u)) = \eta = X\tau+u

and the model for the marks as

g(E(Y|X,u)) = \alpha + \beta * \eta
                    =\alpha + \beta * X\tau + \beta * u

Currently, the examples online (Book https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/ch-lcox.html#model-fitting-under-preferential-sampling) show how to add the final term, but not the term with the fixed effects.

I'd settle for a model with a separate parameter for fixed and random contributions, viz

g(E(Y|X,u)) = \alpha + \beta_f * X\tau + \beta_r * u

with \beta_f != \beta_r, but it would be nice to have the option.

Any advice would be greatly appreciated.  I'm a bit lost right now.

Thanks in advance,

Scott

messages.subject: Sum-to-zero constraints across effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi

Apologies if this is answered somewhere in the documentation.

We have a spatio-temporal problem we are working on where we stack several latent random effects, like:

formula = y ~ -1 + f(name_1, model = SPDE_1, group = ...) + f(name_2, model = SPDE_2, group = ...)

I understand that for each effect INLA can force a sum to zero using constr=TRUE, or by setting an extra constraint, e.g.
A <- matrix(1, ncol = n, nrow = 1)
 <https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-mixed.html#cb103-2>e <- rep(0, 1)
formula = y ~ -1 + f(name_1, model = SPDE_1, group = ..., extraconstr = list(A,e)) + ...

Is there a way to apply a sum constraint across multiple effects, i.e. A[f1 f2 ... fn] = e. I see that the linear combination can be calculated across effects using
inla.make.lincomb(  <https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-INLAfeatures.html#cb194-2> name_1 = A1, name_2 = A2 ...), but can this be used to force a constraint on model across effects?

Thanks in advance,
Sam Royston
Uni of Bristol.

messages.body_plain:
if you want the difference point-wise, you can sample for each marginal
(using inla.rmarginal) and do the difference (pointwise). this will
ignore any dependence between the two fitted values, in case there is
any (this would be model spesific).

The 'correct' way is to include the dependence by defining a joint model
and and study the difference of the linear predictors. but this can be
somewhat tedious.

at least in the simple approach, you'll get the mean difference correct

g( E(Y|u)) = \eta_Y
             = W_Y\tau + u_Y

where W_Y is a design matrix for the covariates at the sites X, \tau is a vector of coefficients and u_Y is a vector containing realisations of a Gaussian process at sites X.  This is 'just' a standard geostatistical model for the marks

The model for the point process allows for possible preferential sampling. It is

log( E(X|u)) = \alpha + \beta*\eta
             = \alpha + \beta*W_X\tau + \beta*u

where W_X is a design matrix (dimension M_X \times p) that depends upon the approximation to the Poisson point process (on- or off-grid, for example), \tau and u are as before, \alpha is a constant and \beta is a preference parameter.  If \beta>0 then the sites are associated with higher values of E(Y|u).

Please note that, since last email, I have swapped \beta and \alpha so that they now affect the locations and not the marks.  The same problem persists though (this is just a rescaling to make the preference more obvious).

Note that in the INLA call, the design matrix will be of dimension (|X|+M_X) \times p, to allow for the two outcomes and will consist of the two W matrices above being stacked.

Adding in the scalar parameter \alpha is easy, as it involves only adding a column of |X| zeros and |M_X| ones to the design matrix fed into INLA.

Adding \beta is where my confusion lies.  If it were known a priori then I could simply multiply the relevant part of the design matrix.  If it were additive, then I could add columns to the design matrix (like \alpha).  In the model for the locations, the design matrix retains the p columns but the coefficients are now \beta*\tau -- a 'compound' parameter (my made-up term).

So, I don't think that the model can be specified by altering the design matrix -- the terms of interest are 'compound' parameters, not additive.  The \beta scalar parameter also spans many covariates (columns of the design matrix).

I read the helpfile for f() to indicate that it applies only to single covariates, not multiple ones as needed here.

Am I missing something? Is this even possible as it is a non-linear model (just)?

Thanks again,

Scott

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
You can do it also using lincombs (if not many) or considering samples from the joint posterior. Considering the inla.make.lincombs() function you can specify a set of contrasts you want and it will be computed by inla(). By considering the posterior samples, using inla.posterior.sample() you can do it by post-processing the samples from the linear predictor.
Elias

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Grouped splines
messages.body_plain:
The f(value, weights, …) syntax means
  Effect[i] = weights[i] * latent(value[i])
In the model=“iid” case that gives you “random slopes”, and in the rw2 case you get “splines” (really an integrated random walk Gaussian process, which isn’t exactly the same thing as a spline, which specifically refers to the corresponding penalty minimiser) multiplied by the weighs, sometimes referred to as varying coefficient models.

It sounds like you’re looking for a model with a rw2 process of one variable, replicated across another, index, variable?
Then you want
f(continuous_var, model=“rw2”, replicate = index)
?
If you spell out the model you want in equations it should be easier to figure out precisely what model you want; there is no universal terminology across all application fields, and the same vague description based on code examples can refer to very different actual models, so describing them in unambiguous maths is often necessary.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hello INLA users,

I've been thinking about the possibility of implementing INLA for genomic analysis (via R-INLA package), such as Bayes A/B/A*B/Lasso, Ridge Regression and so on.

(as far as I understand, shrinkBayes only copes with RNA data, right?)

Is it feasible? Do INLA have any restrictions (that may have passed trough my thoughts unnoticed) that could impair it's capability to deal with this kind of models?

Thank you very much in advance.

messages.subject: Re: Genomic selection
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paoulo,

You can fit ridge regression model on marker covariates (aka SNP-BLUP in genomics) by using INLA's Z-matrix model. You can also fit a model with a user-defined precision matrix (aka G-BLUP in genomics) by using INLA's generic models. Some examples of using INLA for such (or similar models) are:

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00122-019-03424-y
https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/217/3/iyab002/6117210
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33519886/
https://gsejournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12711-020-00588-w

You can not fit non-Gaussian "flexible" priors such as the "BayesWhatever" models in genomics with INLA to my understanding. In most cases there isn't much difference between the SNP-BLUP and BayesWhatever so just run SNP-BLUP;)

INLA does struggle with these dense genomic models though because it is optimised for sparse models, such as pedigree-based models, time-series models, SPDE, etc.

messages.subject: Problem with different coordinates
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone!
I have a problem which is for me quite incomprehensible.
I am fitting the usual spatio_temporal model for polllution data, based on the SPDE approach, in order to predict the concentration of pollutant over time.
At first I used LAT/LONG coordinates for the data (coordinates of measurment stations and borders of my region  of interest) and everything was good. I could process a mesh of 515 nodes during a time of 180 days for 49 stations.
The problem though was that that the range posterior mean (for the spde) was uninterpretable.
So I thought to convert the coordinates in UTM, in order to have a km-unit range.
It works well with coarse meshes and for a small period of time, but when I run more complex model It does not work anymore.
The issue is that with same (or similar) time and mesh dimensions, LAT/LONG system works fine while for UTM it doesn't.
Is there a reason or am I missing something about the coordinate-systems?

PS1: the plots of mesh are good with UTM
PS2: the posterior mean of range in the case of the UTM model small enough to fit was good and reasonable

I post below the error (that ususally results when I'm trying to fit too big models)

Thank you very much,
Alessandro

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Problem with different coordinates
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
that shouldn't be an issue; check that all of your objects and units are in the same crs (mesh, boundary, input data, etc).,
and check your psde prior settings, so that they are reasonable for the coordinate system you're in.

The data given to inla() should end up being very similar in your two cases, so it's not clear what the source of the issue might be, except for model resolution and/or some forgotten coordinate conversions.

PS. There will soon be a version of inlabru with expanded support for sf, including more robust coordinate transformations etc.  The INLA package itself will also get some of these enhancements.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
I do not think the 'selection' argument in posterior.sample was that
great of an idea as it onle save storage not computational cost, and it
just lead to confusion, so...

I rather prefer to just use inla.posterior.sample.eval to exact terms
you like. there is a vignette about this function, please check (need
new testing version).

there is an example

n <- 100
x <- rnorm(n)
xx <- rnorm(n)
y <- rnorm(n)

r <- inla(y ~ 1 + x*xx,
          data = data.frame(y, x, xx),
          control.compute = list(config = TRUE))

fun <- function() {
    return (c(x, xx, get("x:xx")))
}

xx <- inla.posterior.sample(1000, r)
coeffs <- inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun, xx)

the log likelihood is given by:

L(Beta)det(X'WX)^0.5,

see e.g slide 10 in https://www.eio.upc.edu/ca/seminari/docs/georg-heinze-logistics-regression-with-rare-events-problems-and-solutions.pdf

I have a situation where there are very few "positive" cases, 320 out of 42 000
Any alternatives to Firth's penalized regression that are implemented in INLA?

Best
Fredrik

messages.subject: Neighborhood graph given lots of NA values
messages.subject_clean: Neighborhood graph given lots of NA values
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Say you have data that looks like this map, where there is a lattice
with grid cells and many grid cells have no data. Say you have to make
a CAR model with this data, so you need to deal with a neighborhood
graph. You have a few choices here. You can make a neighborhood graph
with many disconnected subgraphs, and lots of islands (and proceed as
Freni-Sterrantino et al.), or you can make a neighborhood graph using
the full lattice that covers the study area, but enter NA for Y values
in cells with no data. What would you do and why? Do you have any
citations for how to make this decision? I have only found a few
references for dealing with disconnected graphs and they usually focus
on a few singletons or don't otherwise talk about using NA values with
the full lattice.

Thanks,
Tim

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Neighborhood graph given lots of NA values
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Neighborhood graph given lots of NA values
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tim,

if we (for a moment) exclude the bit in Alaska, I would construct a model of the unknown field, based on the full grid, if the grid cells with no data still conceptually exist.
(Depending on why the data there is missing you might need to consider also modelling the missingness mechanism, to avoid bias; there's a paper by Diggle et al from a couple of years ago I think that
discusses issues around preferential sampling).

Reasons:

CAR(1) models only have a well-defined spatial interpretation in the aggregate; see Besag&Mondal 2005 and an earlier Besag paper, both cited in our 2011 SPDE/GMRF paper,
so the only situation a basic equal-neighbour-weights CAR(1) model really makes sense is when space has been split into regions; this is an indirect result from the Besag papers and our SPDE/GMRF paper, that links discrete space models to continuous limits.  So for a process that is _modelled_ on a grid (not necessarily _observed_!) a CAR model can make sense; space is split into a regular patterm of rectangles, and a CAR(1) model is somewhat interpretable.

If one instead builds a CAR model only on the grid boxes that happen to have been observed, any link to the underlying _full_ spatial domain process is lost, and you get
a purely ad hoc model construction that does induce some dependence between the data sites, but no consistency with respect to the observation pattern.
Consider the case of two years of observation, and a separate model for each year. If the CAR model is based on the observed sites _only_, the two models will be two completely different models,
and even the interpretation of the CAR model parameters can be different.

When possible, I much prefer to work with hierarchical model constructions where the estimands exist independently of any observations.
This is also a framework in which, conceptually, "mis-aligned data" is simply converted into multiple ways in which a common latent "truth" can be connected to different observation systems.

FInally, what about Alaska? One could make a grid with slightly irregular outline to stretch out to Alaska; this basically is the same thing as an SPDE model with alpha=1 (no pointwise evaluation meaning, but well defined for spatial integration such as pixels; see the Besag papers), so from this the step isn't far to being able to use models other process smoothnesses; the SPDE/GMRF connection was partly developed to show how CAR(p) model parameters _should_ be constructed so that the resulting models become as invariant to the source locations as possible.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
I am struggling to find INLA example code to addess the problem I am trying to solve.

I have a spatial dataset with irregularly shapled polygons containing diseased animal polgygons. Most have no bounding polygon with a diseased animal but some do (ie mostly islands). Some polygons in a particular region of the map contain poison bait counts (also mostly 'islands').

I am trying to
1) determine the spatial cluserting of diseased animals relative to a background expected rate. Similar to say using a Ripleys K function on point data relative to a Poisson point process.
2) determine any spatial correlation (eg via a p value) of diseased animal polygons to bait polygons.

Any suggestions for models to use and tutorials/example code would be appreciated
